extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in philosophy, epistemology, and liberal education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria Russell advances for good philosophical method (relation of intuition, intellect, logic, time, ethics) and for the role of science in a liberal education. Focuses on standards for thought, argument, and pedagogical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallibility of intuition / Need for intellectual scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition, though subjectively convincing while present, is at least as fallible as intellect; its greater subjective certainty is a demerit because it makes it more irresistibly deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-knowledge (people are often unconscious of their own meannesses), love (apparent insight into another's soul is often illusory). Therefore intuitions should be examined and not accepted merely because they feel certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation supplies novelty; intellect best handles novel data
rubrics_metrics.description: New and unique data are given in sensation rather than by a special faculty of intuition; intellect, not intuition, is much more capable of dealing with data that are new in a remarkable manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the hen that seems 'inside' her ducklings becomes helpless when ducklings behave differently (go to water). When surroundings change, intellect’s slower, analytic methods are more reliable than instinctive intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of intuition as an aspect of instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuition is an aspect and development of instinct: admirable in customary surroundings which have moulded habits, but incompetent when circumstances require non-habitual responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize the success of intuition in ordinary, instinct-shaped tasks to domains (like philosophy) that demand non-habitual modes of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy requires disinterestedness and intellectual aloofness
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy, aiming at theoretical understanding, is a refined, highly civilised pursuit demanding liberation from the life of instinct and a certain aloofness from mundane hopes and fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick, unanalysed convictions (intuition) are least deserving of acceptance in philosophy because philosophical objects are strange, unusual, and remote; a habit of reflective, disinterested thought is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic must be candid and not designed to justify pre-existing convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person has a mystic conviction and then seeks logical grounds for it, the logic that results will be hospitable to any ground that suggests itself and thus biased; logic must not be used to vindicate a prior belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware 'malicious' logic that reads Nature with the conviction that it is all illusion; to make the common world intelligible, argument must be honest, not hostile or pre-judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical doctrines should account for scientific and common-sense facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical systems that render philosophers incapable of giving any account of the world of science and daily life are defective; philosophers should not be complacent about inconsistency with well-established facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one is anxious to understand science and common life, one will discover errors in any doctrine that contradicts them. Logic that denies or ignores established empirical facts is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial contemplation with respect to time
rubrics_metrics.description: Past, present, and future should be treated equally in impartial intellectual contemplation; the felt practical difference between past and future is not an intrinsic metaphysical difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophic truth requires overcoming the attitude that privileges future/planned change; Spinoza: conceiving according to reason affects equally future, past, and present. Avoid 'slavery to time' in philosophical outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleological or progress-driven bias (evolutionism) in philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating evolution as a progress toward some better goal allows the notion of time to become a tyrant and introduces practical, ethical preoccupations that are inappropriate for pure philosophical contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that conjectural histories and appeals to development towards good are motivated by practical interests (human destiny) rather than pure philosophical inquiry; philosophy should maintain impartiality instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should not claim the empirical province of special sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions about the future or about very particular empirical matters belong to particular sciences and should be ascertained by their methods rather than by philosophical conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must have its own province—questions other sciences can neither prove nor disprove—and must not act as a shortcut to results properly obtained by empirical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical neutrality in philosophical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should aim at an ethically neutral standpoint: distinctions of good and evil belong to action and psychological particulars, not to the abstract province of philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ethical concerns may inspire study, they must not obtrude into philosophical detail. Treat love and hate as analogous attitudes toward objects rather than as fundamentally different theoretical categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish subjective emotional revelation from metaphysical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystic emotion reveals a possibility of human nature (a feeling of universal love and joy) but does not, by itself, reveal facts about the non-human or about the universe in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take emotional revelations as metaphysical proof; account for the fact that higher goods perceived in mystic vision may be reflections of our emotions, not properties of things in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education defined as formation of mental habits and outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Education (in the intended sense) is the formation, by means of instruction, of certain mental habits and a certain outlook on life and the world—not merely the imparting of factual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish this sense from broader (life-education) and narrower (mere instruction) senses; curricular choices should be judged by their capacity to form habits and outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of scientific habit of mind in liberal education
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific habit of mind—patient construction of systems of knowledge, disinterestedness, impersonal outlook, systematic survey, and intellectual curiosity—has intrinsic educational value and should form part of liberal education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science produces cumulative systems unifying detached phenomena (e.g., electromagnetism) that can form the mind as profoundly as classical literature, provided science is taught in a spirit that preserves these aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching method matters: do not reduce science to mere utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent inferiority of scientific education to classical education is not inherent in science but in the spirit in which science is taught—if taught properly, science can produce the highest mental excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid teaching science merely as a collection of useful facts or sensational triumphs; emphasize the leisurely, systematic survey that forms the impersonal and cultured outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive emphasis on the past in education
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely classical education overemphasizes the past and may engender a habit of criticism toward the present and inability to recognize contemporary merit; education should combine appreciation of past and present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate impartiality that allows recognizing value in contemporary and future achievements, not only esteem for the completed past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic modesty and acceptance of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy should be modest, piecemeal, and arduous—less concerned to flatter hopes about human destiny and more capable of accepting the world without imposing temporary human demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modest outlook parallels scientific submission to facts; insistence on external realisation of the good is a form of self-assertion that can impair inward goods and reverence toward fact.
